en: The Sūtra on the Transformation of the Female Body, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Jibin during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
There was a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus and eight thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom were well-known to the public.

Some had come from other buddha-fields to attend the gathering, as did devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, together with hundreds of thousands of their retinues, all having come to the assembly.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly as he preached the Dharma; his words were excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end. The phrasing and meaning were skillful and subtle, fully elucidating the characteristics of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
At that time, there was in the assembly a brahmin named Sudatta; his wife, Viśuddhadivākarī, who was carrying a female fetus, sat among the crowd.

Although the girl she carried remained within the womb, her sense faculties were fully developed and untainted by impurities; with single-minded devotion, she joined her palms toward the Buddha to listen to the Dharma, desiring to ask a question.

At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha, having attained the pure and clear divine eye that transcends the human eye and perceives neither increase nor decrease, saw a woman conceived within the body of Viśvabhū. Her faculties were complete and untainted by impurity; with single-minded devotion, she joined her palms toward the Buddha to listen to the Dharma, desiring to ask a question.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha, having witnessed this event, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

This daughter conceived by Viśuddhasūrya possesses all her faculties complete and is untainted by impurity; with single-minded devotion she joins her palms toward the Buddha to listen to the Dharma, desiring to ask a question."
The Buddha said:
"Aniruddha! I clearly perceived this girl while she was in the womb, yet I did not speak of it."
"Why is this? If there are sentient beings who do not believe in the Tathāgata’s words of truth and sincerity, these people will undergo great suffering and affliction for a long night!
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance, universally illuminating the trichiliocosm so that it was entirely pervaded.

Furthermore, by means of his supernatural power, he caused this entire assembly to see that the girl was within her mother’s womb, with all her faculties complete and untainted by impurity, single-mindedly joining her palms toward the Buddha to listen to the Dharma and wishing to ask a question.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a sound that all sentient beings delight in hearing—
a sound that was pure, namely: a sound easy to understand, a straightforward sound, a pure sound, a faultless sound pleasing to the faculty of hearing,
a sound capable of producing joy in body and mind, and a sound free from all disturbances like the clarity of a pure [mirror].
A voice like the moon; a voice of exquisite beauty that flows on without interruption; a voice that is not coarse or harsh;
a voice that skillfully enters the hearts of people and can remove greed, hatred, and delusion; a voice that causes others to rejoice and find faith and delight;
a voice surpassing that of Brahmā; a voice like the roll of thunder; a voice like celestial music; a voice like the roar of a lion.
With voices that proclaim the Dharma and voices that are the fruit of roots of goodness accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* *nayuta* eons—
using such harmonious and elegant sounds, he addressed the woman, saying:
"For what purpose have you come to listen and receive [the teaching], and what do you wish to ask?
By the Buddha's majestic power, the girl spoke to the Buddha from within her womb:
"World-Honored One!"

There are sentient beings who are greedily attached to the view of a self, engaging in false conceptualization born of inversion—where there is no sentient being, they give rise to the notion of a sentient being; where there is no self, they reckon it as a self; and where there is no life-principle (jīva), no person (pudgala), and no nourishing entity (poṣa), they reckon them as a life-principle, a person, and a nourishing entity. It is for the sake of such sentient beings that I wish to ask a question.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are greedily attached to the view of self and are unable to comprehend the Single Vehicle path; [the Buddha] desires to awaken them to the Single Vehicle path.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are shrouded and bound by ignorance and craving for existence, and are unable to comprehend the Dharma of clear knowledge and liberation; [the Buddha] desires to cause them to comprehend clear knowledge and liberation.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are shrouded and obscured by greed, anger, and the blindness of ignorance, such that they are unable to advance toward and seek the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; it is for the sake of causing them to cultivate and realize these three gates of liberation.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who have fallen into the four inversions: they perceive the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure. In order to explain the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to them—namely, that "this is suffering," "this is the origin of suffering," "this is the cessation of suffering," and "this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering"—[the Buddha appears].

"Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are shrouded by the five hindrances and do not cultivate the five faculties; [the Buddha] desires to cause them to fulfill the dharmas of the five faculties.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are greedily dependent on the six sense bases and have not realized the six supernormal powers; [the Buddha] desires to explain the dharmas of the six supernormal powers for their sake."

"Furthermore, there are sentient beings who delight in the seven stations of consciousness but cannot clearly understand the seven factors of enlightenment; I wish to explain these seven factors of awakening for them.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who practice the eightfold wrong path but cannot comprehend the eightfold noble path; I wish to explain the factors of the noble path for them."

Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose minds harbor the nine afflictions and who are unable to enter the nine successive attainments; it is for their sake that I wish to explain the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who abide in the ten unwholesome paths of action and are unable to diligently cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action; [the Buddha] desires to cause them to fulfill these ten wholesome paths.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who have fallen into the assembly of the wrong or the indeterminate, and thus are not vessels for the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) dharmas; [the Buddha] desires to cause them to clearly understand the dharmas of the right assembly. Desiring to cause sentient beings to accomplish roots of goodness and to achieve self-subjugation, he preaches the Dharma according to their various aspirations and requests.
“World-Honored One!
For the sake of such causes and conditions as these, I now wish to ask a question of the Buddha while listening to the Dharma.
At that time, the entire assembly marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and spoke these words:
“The Dharma of the Tathāgata is truly rare!
Although the Bodhisattva remains within the womb, his benefit to sentient beings through the proclamation of the Dharma never ceases.
If there are good men or good women who see or hear him, who among them would not resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
At that time, by the supernatural power of the Buddha, this girl was suddenly born through transformation from her mother’s right side, like a bodhisattva in their final existence.
By the power of the causes and conditions of this girl’s merit and wisdom, her mother’s body was freed from all afflictions and ailments, and she was restored to her former state.

Not long after the girl was born, the earth shook with a great trembling, a rain of various celestial flowers fell, and all musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck. Upon the land, flowers grew as large as chariot wheels, adorned in every way with exquisite colors and fragrances that delighted the hearts of men; they had a hundred or a thousand petals, with stems of gold, leaves of silver, filaments of agate, and bases of red pearls.

The girl stood atop him; her physical form was like that of a child of two or three years, her countenance was upright and refined, and she was most lovely and venerable—all of which arose from the karmic retribution of wholesome deeds in previous lives.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra took celestial garments and necklaces, went to her place, and said to her:
"Noble lady! Put on these garments and necklaces; do not stand there naked!"
The woman replied to Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
"A bodhisattva does not adorn himself with such garments and necklaces. Why is this? Because..."
A Bodhisattva constantly uses the mind of enlightenment as their clothing and ornaments to adorn themselves; thus, they surpass all the adornments of the gods and humans in the world.
"Furthermore, Kauśika,
there are ten kinds of garments and ornaments with which a bodhisattva adorns themselves.
What are these ten?
This means not losing the mind of enlightenment, never forgetting or abandoning the profound resolve;
constantly employing great loving-kindness to act as a protector and refuge for all sentient beings;
taking great compassion as the foundation, and practicing with diligent perseverance.
To deliver all sentient beings, never abandoning them, and to bring all sentient beings to fulfillment;
to constantly adorn the actions of body, speech, and mind with a sense of shame and remorse;
and to give away all things without expecting any reward.
They maintain all precepts and ascetic practices (*dhūta-guṇa*), never transgressing them;
they abide in the power of patience, able to endure what is difficult to endure;
and they seek supreme roots of goodness through right skillful means.
Although their minds abide within various samādhis such as the dhyānas and the immeasurables, they never seek to realize untimely liberation.
Kauśika! These are called the ten kinds of clothing, necklaces, and ornaments of a bodhisattva, which they never depart from at any time.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
A bodhisattva adorns his body with the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana), which surpass all other ornaments; yet these marks arise from merit and wisdom."
What are merit and wisdom?

They consist of being able to relinquish various cherished objects through diverse acts of giving to others; maintaining a mind free from malice or resentment toward all sentient beings; constantly seeking virtuous conduct; not limiting one's giving but ensuring others are fully satisfied; and regarding all sentient beings as fields of merit.
Kauśika! This is called the first adornment of robes and necklaces for a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva wishes to realize the vehicle of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, it is not called an adornment.

If one dwells in a mind of stinginess, a mind of broken precepts, a mind of malice, a mind of indolence, a mind of distracted thought, or a base and inferior mind mixed with various afflictions and wrong wisdom, thinking, "I cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi," and thus being struck with alarm, fear, regret, and remorse—this is not the adornment of a bodhisattva.
"Why is this? Because they have distanced themselves from the dharmas that adorn a bodhisattva.

At that time, having heard this discourse on the various dharmas that adorn a bodhisattva, twelve thousand devas and humans who had previously planted roots of goodness all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to this girl,
"You may accept these garments and necklaces from Śakra-devānām-indra.
The girl addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to receive it. Why is this? Because—”
Sharing the same aspirations as I, they should likewise be adorned with identical robes and necklaces;
yet this Śakra seeks only limited wisdom, his inclinations are base, he is weary of birth and death, constantly harbors fear, and desires to enter nirvāṇa quickly;
he always receives the essentials of the Dharma from others, and the light of his wisdom illuminates only himself, failing to reach others.
Like one who grasps a bundle of grass while attempting to cross a river, they cannot serve as a pure field of merit for others;
forever separated from the pure eye of wisdom of all Buddhas, they cannot clearly understand the faculties of sentient beings.
"Bhagavān!

I now don the firm armor, aspiring for the Mahāyāna and desiring to benefit all beings. I shall assemble the great Dharma-ship to ferry across those who have not yet crossed, seek spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) to turn the wheel of Dharma, and have no expectations of anything from others. Adorned with the wisdom of the Tathāgata, I shall also cause all beings to attain the pure eye of wisdom of all Buddhas."
“World-Honored One!
I have come from that land to be born here in this world, desiring to see the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, to pay homage and make offerings, and to hear his preaching of the Dharma.”
"That Buddha, the World-Honored One, shall personally provide me with robes and necklaces so that I may wear them.
At that time, the assembly of devas and humans all had this thought:
"What is the name of the world from which this girl has come?"
How far is it from here? In which direction does it lie?
What is the name of the Tathāgata in that land?
Is he currently present there, preaching the Dharma and teaching?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of this assembly, addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"To the southeast of this world-system, passing beyond thirty-six nayutas of buddha-fields, there is a world named Pure Abode (Vimalavihāra). There dwells a Buddha named Vimalakīrtirāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma."

Śāriputra! This girl has passed away from the world of Pure Abode and been reborn here in this realm, desiring to bring sentient beings to maturity, and also wishing to pay homage, make offerings to me, and listen to my teaching of the Dharma.

After the Buddha had spoken these words, before long, the Tathāgata Vimalakīrtirāja conceived a heart of compassion and, by means of his supernormal powers, sent the robes, necklaces, and ornaments worn by those bodhisattvas to appear before the women, suspending them in mid-air. He then uttered this voice:
"O virtuous daughters! "
The Tathāgata Vimalakīrtirāja of the world-system Viśuddhavihāra has sent these robes and necklaces for you; you should wear them, just as the bodhisattvas here do.
"If you put on these garments and ornaments for adornment, you shall immediately attain all five supernormal powers; you too should do as I have!
At that moment, the girl took the garments and ornaments from the air and immediately put them on.

In an instant, the garments and necklaces emitted wondrous radiance; with the exception of the Tathāgata’s light, the splendors of all other Brahmās, Śakras, the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings, the sun, and the moon were no longer visible.
At that moment, the girl was endowed with the five supernormal powers; she descended from the lotus pedestal and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
As she lifted her feet and set them down, the great earth immediately shook in six ways.
Having arrived before the Buddha, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha seven times, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I pray that the Tathāgata will expound for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the Dharma of gathering awakening and increasing it, so that these bodhisattvas shall not regress from the unsurpassed path, shall transcend the activities of Māra, and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed this girl, saying:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they can grasp awakening and cause it to increase.
What are these four?"
First, the pure mind;
second, the profound mind;
third, skillful means.
Fourth, not abandoning the bodhicitta.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, one should constantly desire to benefit all sentient beings;
second, one should always maintain a compassionate heart and have pity for all sentient beings;
third, one should deliver and liberate sentient beings through great compassion.
Fourth, through firm and resolute diligence, one fulfills all Buddha-dharmas. These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, by discerning all phenomena, one generates great faith;
second, one remains far removed from the mindsets of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
third, one delights in observing the supreme Dharma, desiring to fully perfect all Buddha-dharmas.
Fourth, by practicing with diligent vigor, one will certainly achieve its fruit.
These are called the four.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, to be free from arrogance;
second, to eliminate the conceited mind;
third, to respect and honor one's elders and superiors.
Fourth, being easy to instruct and admonish.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, one does not give rise to anger or resentment toward those who come seeking;
second, one relinquishes all things without seeking their reward;
third, one has no regrets after having given.
Fourth, to dedicate all roots of goodness toward enlightenment.
These are the four. Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, not breaking the precepts;
second, not piercing the precepts;
third, not defiling the precepts.
Fourth is the precept of non-turbidity.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, their nature is harmonious and they are able to endure;
second, they skillfully protect the intentions of others;
third, they protect their own bodies and never transgress against others.
Fourth, dedication toward bodhi.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, firm and steadfast diligence;
second, clear and pure diligence;
third, undaunted diligence.
Fourth, dedication toward enlightenment.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, physical strength and capability;
second, mental strength and capability;
third, the ability to skillfully cultivate and accumulate the various dhyānas and their factors.
Fourth, never forgetting or losing the bodhicitta.
These are called the four.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, generosity;
second, pleasant speech;
third, beneficial action;
The fourth is sameness of purpose (samānārthatā).
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, the mind of loving-kindness pervades all places;
second, great compassion is free from weariness;
third, the mind of sympathetic joy deeply loves and reveres the Dharma.
Fourth, the mind of equanimity is free from both aversion and attachment.
These are called the four.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, listening to the Dharma without weariness;
second, correctly contemplating and reflecting upon it;
third, being able to practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Fourth, dedication toward enlightenment.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, knowing that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
second, definitively knowing that the aggregates are suffering;
third, definitively knowing that all dharmas are without self.
Fourth, to know with certainty that nirvāṇa is the dharma of quiescence.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, not rejoicing when gaining profit;
second, not grieving when losing profit;
third, maintaining a mind that is always equanimous even though one possesses a reputation.
Fourth, although one hears an evil reputation, the mind is not troubled.
These are the four. "Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, not becoming angry when reviled by others;
second, not being delighted when praised;
third, being able to endure suffering when encountering it.
Fourth, although one delights in pleasure, one does not indulge in negligence, nor does one disparage others.
These are called the four.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, contemplating causes;
second, knowing effects;
third, departing from the views of the two extremes.
Fourth, awakening to the principle of dependent origination.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, knowing that there is no self within;
second, knowing that there are no sentient beings without;
third, knowing that there is no life-span in both the internal and external.
Fourth, ultimate purity and the absence of a person.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, practicing emptiness without fear;
second, contemplating signlessness without sinking;
third, being without discrimination regarding wishlessness.
Fourth, to contemplate all phenomena as being without volitional activity.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are another four dharmas:
First, not realizing the knowledge of suffering;
second, not realizing the knowledge of the origin;
third, not realizing the knowledge of cessation;
Fourth, not realizing the knowledge of the path.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, to contemplate enlightenment deeply;
second, not to slander the true Dharma;
third, to remain within the ranks of the Saṃgha and never regress.
Fourth, not giving rise to disputes regarding the Dharma. These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, it causes lustful desire not to arise;
second, it does not engage in objective clinging;
third, it cuts off lustful desire, hatred, and delusion.
Fourth, the remaining afflictions are likewise so;
these are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, one’s mind is always impartial toward all sentient beings;
second, one regards all sentient beings equally as fields of merit;
third, one views both the Buddhas and sentient beings as entirely equal.
Fourth, both phenomena and sentient beings are entirely equal.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are another four dharmas:
First, not to exalt oneself;
second, not to disparage others;
third, not to look down upon those who have not yet studied.
Fourth, one should love and respect those who have already trained as if they were teachers.
These are called the four.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, to distance oneself from useless speech;
second, to constantly seek solitude and stillness;
third, to delight in dwelling in araṇya hermitages without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
Fourth, diligently seeking the various merits and benefits of the araṇya.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are another four dharmas:
First, having few desires;
second, knowing contentment;
third, knowing the proper measure regarding pure things.
"Fourth, one delights in practicing the dhūta austerities and does not crave superior or exquisite clothing and food.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are another four dharmas:"
First, knowing oneself;
second, knowing others;
third, knowing the proper time.
Fourth is knowing the meaning.
These are called the four.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, delighting in the Dharma;
second, delighting in its meaning;
third, delighting in the truths.
Fourth, delighting in the accomplishment of sentient beings.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, internal purity, which is able to protect one's own mind;
second, external purity, which is able to protect sentient beings;
third, the purity of the Dharma, which is the sphere for practicing goodness.
Fourth, through the purity of wisdom, one is able to abandon arrogance.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, detachment from the self;
second, removal of what belongs to the self;
third, elimination of all views.
Fourth, the severing of craving and aversion.
These are called the four.
"Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
First, skillful means encompassing wisdom;
second, wisdom encompassing skillful means;
third, great compassion encompassing all forms of giving.
Fourth, diligence encompasses all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
"Good daughter!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they are able to encompass awakening and cause it to increase."
At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these four dharmas— which can encompass and cause the increase of bodhi—
thirty-two thousand devas and humans in the assembly all resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the girl:
"What name did your parents give you?
Then the girl replied:
“Venerable Śāriputra!
All dharmas are fundamentally without names; although names are established in accordance with conceptual discrimination, they are not real, for there is no fixed master.”
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva receives a name according to their practice:
if they attain a pure mind, they are called "one of pure mind."
If one attains the profound mind, they are called one with a profound mind;
if one practices skillful means, they are called one with pure skillful means;
if one practices giving, they are called one who is well able to give.
If one cultivates ethical discipline, they are called one of pure precepts;
if one abides in patience, they are called one who possesses the power of forbearance;
if one exerts diligent effort, they are called one who has donned the armor of vigor.
If one dwells in the various dhyānas, one is called "Constant Samādhi";
if one attains wisdom, one is called "Great Wisdom";
if one dwells in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, one is called "Great Loving-Kindness, Great Compassion, Great Sympathetic Joy, and Great Equanimity."
If one dwells in an araṇya, they are called one who lives in seclusion and free from affairs;
if one does not abandon the dhūta practices, they are called one who practices pure merit;
if one delights in gathering wholesome dharmas, they are called one who joyfully seeks the Dharma.
"To speak briefly, she has received this name because she set out upon the Mahāyāna by means of whatever roots of goodness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"When this girl put on her robes and ornaments, she emitted a great radiance that shone universally upon the great assembly; for this reason, this girl is named Vimalaprabhā (Stainless Light), and you should remember and uphold this."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again asked the girl Vimalaprabhā:
“Did you receive this female body from the presence of the Buddha Vimalakīrtirāja in the world Pure Abode and come here?”
The woman Vimalaprabhā replied to the venerable Śāriputra,
“In that buddha-world there are no women.
Śāriputra said:
"Why have you now come to be born in this place in the form of a woman?
The woman replied,
"I have not come to be born in this place by means of a male form or a female form, nor by means of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Why is this so? Venerable Śāriputra, what do you think?
Does a person created by the Tathāgata as a transformation, traveling from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field, possess any distinguishing marks of gender, aggregates, elements, or sense-bases?
Śāriputra said: "No! Why is this so? Because..."
"The emanations of the Tathāgata are without distinction.
The woman said,
"Venerable Śāriputra!"
Just as there is no distinction among those emanated by the Tathāgata, so all phenomena are entirely like emanations;
if one knows that all phenomena share the same characteristic as an emanation, then from one buddha-field to another buddha-field, one perceives no distinction.
Śāriputra said:
"Since you perceive no differentiation among all phenomena, how can you bring sentient beings to maturity?
The woman replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
If one perceives distinctions among all phenomena, one will be unable to bring sentient beings to maturity;
if one does not perceive distinctions among all phenomena, one will certainly be able to bring sentient beings to maturity."
Śāriputra asked the girl,
“How many sentient beings have you now brought to maturity?
The girl replied:
“Just as the afflictions have been severed by the Venerable Śāriputra. Śāriputra said:
“The nature of the afflictions that I have severed is non-existent.”
The woman said,
“The nature of sentient beings is likewise non-existent.
Śāriputra said:
"What can sentient beings who lack intrinsic nature accomplish?
The woman replied,
"If afflictions lack intrinsic nature, what more is there to be severed?"
Śāriputra said,
"Because there is no conceptual differentiation, this is called 'cessation'.
The girl said:
“As the Venerable Śāriputra has said, if one does not discriminate between self and other, this too is called ‘accomplishing sentient beings.
Śāriputra then asked the woman,
“What is meant by ‘accomplishing sentient beings’?”
The woman replied,
“To not give rise to defiled attachment within any state of existence— this is called the accomplishment of sentient beings.
Śāriputra then asked the woman again:
“Among the three vehicles, by which vehicle do you bring sentient beings to maturity?
The woman replied, “Venerable Śāriputra! ”

For example, when sweet rain falls equally from the sky, it causes all seeds, sprouts, medicinal herbs, and trees—whether superior, middling, or inferior—to grow; does that rain possess any marks of discrimination?
Śāriputra said:
"Although that water can cause crops to grow, it has no discrimination.
[The Buddha replied: "It is so, Śāriputra!"

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas likewise have no discrimination regarding the Dharma they teach; rather, they discipline those among sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured for the path of the Three Vehicles.
Śāriputra again asked the girl:
"How does one tame? What is the meaning of that?"
Then the woman replied:
"As for what is called 'subduing,' it is the ability to perceive that the deviant path is itself the right path;
this is named subduing. Why is this so? Because..."
Ordinary beings, being subject to perversion, are unable to contemplate correctly and are therefore not disciplined.
If one contemplates the mark of equality within the false paths and neither follows nor aspires to those false paths, this is called ultimate discipline.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that which is called "subduing" refers to both self and non-self; this too is called subduing. Why is this so?
"One who has no view of self does not crave or give rise to any afflictions; this is called liberation.
The woman asked Śāriputra, "Has the Venerable One attained liberation?"
Śāriputra said,
"I have attained liberation.
The girl said:
"Who binds you that you speak of attaining liberation?

Śāriputra replied, "There is no one who binds me such that I attain liberation; rather, its intrinsic nature is the characteristic of liberation. For this reason, I say that I have attained liberation."
The woman said, "If its intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, this is the characteristic of liberation; why then do you say, 'I have attained liberation'?
Śāriputra replied:
"All dharmas possess the characteristic of liberation; therefore, I say that I have attained liberation.
The woman said:
"As the Venerable Śāriputra has stated, if one knows that all dharmas possess the characteristic of liberation, this is precisely what is called ultimate liberation."
Śāriputra said: "What you have just spoken is no different from what has been spoken by Arhats whose outflows are exhausted.
The woman said:
“Venerable Śāriputra!
Now I, too, am an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
Śāriputra said:
“For what reason do you say this?
The woman replied:

“I too am far removed from all dust and defilement; regarding all the factors of the path belonging to pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, I fully know and see them, yet I do not desire or delight in them, seeking only the wisdom of a Buddha.”
Therefore, I say: "This one is an Arhat!
All outflows have been exhausted."
Śāriputra asked: "Is there any cause or condition by which bodhisattvas become arhats?
The woman replied:
"Yes," Śāriputra said,
"by what conditions does it exist?"
The woman said:

"If there are sentient beings who have previously planted roots of goodness and should be liberated by means of the body of a śrāvaka, she immediately manifests the body of a śrāvaka and speaks these words: 'I am an arhat!'"
"For the sake of sentient beings, he teaches the Dharma for realizing arhatship.
This is called a bodhisattva acting as an arhat.
When this teaching was spoken, two hundred bhikṣus were no longer subject to the outflows (āsrava), and their minds attained liberation.
These bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Is this daughter’s eloquence due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, or is it her own power?"
The Buddha said,
"This is due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha!
That girl also possesses the power of her own eloquence."
At that time, the girl Vimalaprabhā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those in this assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—all wish and desire to hear [this teaching].”
By practicing what wholesome deeds can one escape the female body, quickly become a man, and be able to give rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment?
We pray only that the World-Honored One will explain this for us!
At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to benefit and bring accomplishment to the fourfold assembly, addressed the maiden Vimalaprabhā, saying:
"If a woman accomplishes one dharma, she shall be freed from her female body and quickly become a man."
What is meant by "one"?
It refers to seeking bodhi with a profound mind. Why is this so?

If there is a woman who gives rise to the bodhicitta, it is the mind of a person of great goodness, the mind of a great man, the mind of a great seer, and not the mind of an inferior person; it is a mind that forever abandons the narrow and base minds of the two vehicles, a mind capable of refuting the heterodox arguments of external paths, the most supreme mind among those of the three periods of time, and a pure mind capable of eliminating afflictions and being untainted by habitual tendencies.
If women give rise to the bodhicitta, they will no longer harbor minds entangled by the fetters of womanhood.

Because they are no longer so entangled, they will forever leave behind the female body and attain the male form; furthermore, all their roots of goodness should be dedicated toward unexcelled bodhi—this is called the first [practice].
"Furthermore, if a woman accomplishes two dharmas, she can leave behind her female body and quickly become a man.
What are these two? They are:
to eliminate pride, and to be free from deceit and hypocrisy, not practicing illusions or delusions."
"Dedicate all roots of goodness toward unsurpassed bodhi so as to distance oneself from the female body and swiftly become a man; this is called the second.
Furthermore, if a woman accomplishes three dharmas, she can leave the female body behind and swiftly become a man."
What are the three?
First, purity of bodily action, which consists of observing the three precepts of the body;
second, purity of verbal action, which consists of refraining from the four faults of speech.
Third, the purification of mental karma by remaining free from ill-will, wrong views, and delusion.

By means of the roots of goodness produced through these ten wholesome actions, one vows to leave behind the female body, swiftly become a man, and dedicate this toward Bodhi; this is called the third.
"Furthermore, if a woman accomplishes four dharmas, she shall escape the female body and quickly become a man.
What are these four? First, she does not harbor malice or cause harm."
2. Freedom from resentment;
3. Not following after afflictions;
4. Abiding in the power of patience.
These are called the four.
Furthermore, if a woman accomplishes five dharmas, she shall escape the female body and quickly become a man.
What are these five?
First, delighting in the pursuit of wholesome dharmas;
second, honoring the true dharma;
third, finding joy and recreation in the true dharma.
Fourth, to revere those who preach the Dharma as one does one's teachers;
fifth, to practice according to what has been taught.
By means of these roots of goodness, may I be freed from this female body, quickly become a man, and dedicate [these merits] toward Bodhi—these are called the five.
"Furthermore, if a woman accomplishes six dharmas, she shall be freed from her female body and quickly become a man.
What are these six?
First, she constantly recollects the Buddha, vowing to attain the Buddha-body."
2. Constant mindfulness of the Dharma, desiring to turn the wheel of the Dharma;
3. Constant mindfulness of the Saṃgha, desiring to protect and sustain the Saṃgha;
4. Constant mindfulness of the precepts, desiring to fulfill all vows.
Fifth, constantly mindful of giving, desiring to abandon all defilements of affliction;
sixth, constantly mindful of the heavens, desiring to fulfill the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) of the God among Gods.
These are called the six.
Furthermore, if a woman accomplishes seven dharmas, she will escape the female body and quickly become a man.
What are these seven?
First, unshakable faith in the Buddha;
second, unshakable faith in the Dharma;
third, unshakable faith in the Saṅgha.
Fourth, not serving other deities, but revering and honoring only the Buddha;
fifth, not hoarding or being stingy, but being able to act according to one's words;
sixth, having no faults in speech, and always being straightforward and honest.
Seventh, being fully endowed with dignified deportment.
These are called the seven.
"Furthermore, if a woman accomplishes eight dharmas, she shall leave behind her female body and quickly become a man.
What are the eight?
First, not to show partiality toward one's own sons;
second, not to show partiality toward one's own daughters; [and so forth].
Third, not to harbor partiality for her own husband;
fourth, not to be preoccupied with clothing or necklaces;
fifth, not to be greedily attached to floral ornaments or scented unguents.
Sixth, one should not, for the sake of fine food, kill living beings to eat them, as do the rākṣasas;
seventh, one should not be stingy with what one gives, but should always recall such acts with joy;
eighth, one’s conduct should be pure, and one should always maintain a sense of shame and remorse.
These are called the eight.
Furthermore, if a woman accomplishes nine qualities, she shall escape the female body and quickly become a man.
What are these nine?
This refers to the method for pacifying the nine afflictions:
hating those whom I love—having hated them, currently hating them, or about to hate them;
and loving those whom I hate—having loved them, currently loving them, or about to love them.
"Those who have hated me, hate me now, and will hate me in the future—
these are called the nine.
Furthermore, if a woman accomplishes ten qualities, she shall escape the female body and quickly become a man."
What are the ten?
First, not being conceited;
second, eliminating arrogance.
Third, revering one's elders;
fourth, ensuring that all speech is truthful;
fifth, being free from resentment.
Sixth, refraining from harsh speech;
seventh, not being difficult to instruct;
eighth, not being greedy or stingy.
Ninth, not being violent or cruel;
tenth, not being frivolous or playful.
These are called the ten.
"Furthermore, virtuous daughter!
If there is a woman who can contemplate the faults of a woman’s body as they truly are, she will give rise to a mind of weary detachment, swiftly leave the female body, and quickly become a man."
Regarding the faults of the female body: namely, desire, hatred, and delusion, along with other afflictions, are more heavy in women than in men;
furthermore, within this body there are one hundred families of worms that constantly cause suffering and serve as the causes and conditions for grief and distress.
Therefore, because women’s afflictions are particularly heavy, they should reflect and observe well:

this body is a vessel of impurity, filled with foulness and stench; it is like a dried-up well, an empty city, or a ruined village, difficult to find pleasure in. Thus, one should cultivate revulsion toward the body.

Furthermore, contemplate this body as being like a servant, lacking autonomy and constantly afflicted by the necessities of men and women, clothing, food and drink, and household affairs; it must inevitably remove excrement, filth, mucus, and saliva.

For nine months, the child dwells within the womb, subject to manifold afflictions; at the time of birth, one undergoes great agony, barely able to preserve one's life. Therefore, women should give rise to revulsion and detachment toward the female body.

Furthermore, although a woman may be born into a royal palace, she must inevitably belong to another for as long as her life lasts. She is like a maidservant following her master, or like a disciple serving a teacher. Moreover, she suffers from being struck and pelted with various weapons, staves, tiles, stones, and fists, and from being reviled with harsh words; thus, lacking self-mastery amidst such sufferings, a woman should give rise to a mind of weary detachment toward this body.
Furthermore, this female body is constantly bound and confined, just like a snake or a rat within a deep burrow that cannot emerge at will.

Moreover, the regulations for women do not depend upon their own bodies; they must always receive food, drink, clothing, flowers, incense, and various ornaments for adorning the body—such as elephants, horses, and carriages—from others. For these reasons, one ought to cultivate weary detachment toward the female body.

Furthermore, this female body is subject to the commands of others and lacks autonomy; it must perform many tasks—pounding medicinal herbs, husking rice, or roasting and grinding large and small beans and wheat, carding wool, and spinning thread. There are thus immeasurable varieties of such arduous labor; for this reason, women should regard this body with aversion.

"Desiring to be forever free from such manifold sufferings, you should teach this Dharma to others; always bear in mind that the Tathāgata’s words are truthful, and praise the life of renunciation, for it is the way to repay the Buddha's kindness.

You should give rise to this resolve: 'May I leave behind this female body and quickly become a man, so that I may renounce the world and practice the Way within the Buddha-Dharma, no longer craving flower garlands, necklaces, games, gardens, clothing, food, drink, or ornaments for the body.'"
One should contemplate:
one's own body and the retinue standing in attendance are like mechanical wooden puppets, merely being bent, extended, raised, or lowered by the pulling of tendons;
this body is false and deceptive, composed of blood and flesh, and will before long perish and dissolve.
This body is like a latrine, from which nine apertures discharge various kinds of impurities;
this body is composed of the four great elements, yet foolish and ignorant people give rise to attachment toward it;
these aggregates (skandhas) of this body are like enemies.
This body is deceptive and lacks any core of solidity, like an empty village;
this body has no master, being born of father and mother and further adorned by one's own karma;
this body is impure, consisting entirely of putrid filth.
This body is merely a vessel for excrement and urine; it will soon be cast aside and is not a thing to be craved.
This body returns to death, for the out-breath and in-breath must inevitably cease.
This body is without self, like grass, wood, tiles, or stones.
This body has no creator; it arises from causes and conditions.
This body is food for various birds, wolves, dogs, and jackals, as it is cast away among burial mounds.
This body is a mass of suffering, for it is afflicted by four hundred and four diseases.
This body is constantly broken down and dispersed by various ailments such as wind, cold, heat, and their combinations, and it persists only through the power of medicine;
this body is ungrateful, for it knows no satiety in its consumption of food and drink;
this body is insentient, for there is no agent within it.
This body is the final limit, for it must inevitably die.
Therefore, women should observe this body in such a manner as to give rise to a mind of weary detachment and practice wholesome dharmas.

"When practicing wholesome deeds, if one obtains fresh and excellent flowers, fruits, or edible items, one should first offer them to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—the unsurpassed fields of merit—as well as to teachers, preceptors, and parents, and only thereafter eat them oneself."
One should form this thought:
"Just as I now offer these fresh flowers and fruits to a venerable and pure field of merit, may I be freed from this defiled female body and obtain a new and excellent male body."
When the Buddha spoke this Dharma, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs in the assembly all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and spoke these words:
“By all our roots of goodness, may we be freed from female bodies and quickly become men.”

At that time, there were seventy-five householder wives in the assembly who, upon hearing this teaching, felt great joy in their hearts; they immediately took the necklaces they were wearing on their bodies and scattered them over the Buddha.

By the Buddha’s supernatural power, the scattered garlands immediately transformed in mid-air directly above the Buddha’s crown into seventy-five four-pillared jeweled pavilions, which were upright, magnificent, exquisite, and most delightful.

Throughout the entire land of Tai-chung, there were thrones made of various jewels, each occupied by a Tathāgata, naturally manifesting surrounded before and behind by a great assembly of bhikṣus and bodhisattvas.

At that time, the wives of the lay devotees, seeing this divine manifestation, were even more joyful and leaped for joy beyond measure. They approached the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."

We now gather together all our roots of goodness and collectively resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; may we be freed from this female body and likewise dedicate these merits toward supreme enlightenment.
The World-Honored One, out of great compassion, has extensively expounded upon the faults and evils of receiving a female body.
All of it is exactly as the Buddha has spoken; there is nothing therein that is not true.
We shall now diligently cultivate skillful means to forever distance ourselves from such evil transgressions.

From this day forth, for as long as life shall last, I shall uphold the five precepts and purely cultivate the holy life; by these roots of goodness, may I together with all sentient beings attain equal and perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to the laywomen:
"Sisters, it is truly rare that you are able to let out such a great lion's roar!"
"However, do your husbands permit you to practice the holy life?
You should ask them!
The laywomen addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"If we were each to ask our husbands, 'From where did I come to be born here, and from here, where shall I be reborn after passing away?
though they are my husbands, they would be unable to answer; what use, then, would it be to ask?"
Venerable Śāriputra!
If one were to ask the Tathāgata:
"From where did we pass away to be born here in this world? Having passed away from this world, where shall we be born?"
"The Tathāgata perceives this clearly and explains it to us in detail for our sake.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is our father and mother; he is our honored one, our great teacher, our field of merit, and our precious island of refuge."
"Now that we are practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), what is the use of asking about our husbands?
From this day forward, we shall diligently apply skillful means so that we are no longer subject to husbands as other women are."

Why is this? If a person can eliminate the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion, they will never again be afflicted or burdened by them. Now, my body and mind are my husband; is it not a joy for the mind to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*)!
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra!
If one who is not my husband were to take my life while I perceived him as my husband, I would maintain my own mind and purely cultivate the brahma-faring without regret!
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to the housewives:
"You should diligently apply skillful means to leave behind the female body. Why is this? Because..."
"A woman's body cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The wives of the lay devotees said to the Venerable Śāriputra,
"From this day forward, we shall no longer give rise to the afflictions of women."
She immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
Now, before the Buddha, I prostrate my head at your feet; until I have transformed this female body into that of a male, I shall never rise!”
The Buddha said: "Sisters!
I have always said:
"Or there may be women who are able to perform the courageous deeds of men.
However, sisters, if you can practice sixteen dharmas, whatever you wish for shall be obtained according to your intent.
What are the sixteen?
First, purity of ethical discipline;
second, purity of mind.
3. Purity of emptiness;
4. purity of wishlessness;
5. purity of signlessness;
Sixth, purity through non-action;
seventh, knowing that bodily karma is like a shadow;
eighth, knowing that verbal karma is like an echo.
9. Knowing that mental karma is like an illusion;
10. knowing the dharma of dependent origination;
11. being free from the views of the two extremes;
12. Skillfully knowing causes and conditions;
13. Contemplating phenomena as like illusions;
14. Knowing phenomena as like dreams;
"Fifteenth, the nature of marks is like a mirage;
sixteenth, the profound mind is tranquil.
When the Buddha spoke these sixteen dharmas of purity, the great earth shook.

Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the husbands of the seventy-five housewives immediately came to where the Buddha was; each saw his wife prostrating at the Buddha’s feet and asked the Venerable Śāriputra:
"For what reason have our wives just now prostrated at the Buddha’s feet?"
Śāriputra said:

“When these sisters heard the Buddha explain the Dharma for transcending the female body, their hearts were filled with great joy and they leaped for immeasurable delight. They immediately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and for the rest of their lives, they upheld the five precepts and purely cultivated the holy life.”
Now, before the Buddha, I prostrate at his feet and make this vow:
"If I do not transform this female body into that of a man, I shall never rise from here!"
"Furthermore, householders!
You should release these sisters so that they may leave the household life and cultivate the path within the Buddha-dharma.
The householders said:
“As the Venerable One has said, we all wish to go forth.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra!
We now desire to go forth within the Buddha-dharma; please deliver us first, and only afterwards the women.”
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These lay devotees wish to leave the household life within the True Dharma of the Buddha; we pray that the Buddha will grant them permission!”
The Buddha told the householders:
"Within my Dharma, you may go forth as renunciants according to your own wishes.
At that time, the householders addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May you grant us ordination!
The Buddha said,
“Welcome, bhikṣus.”
They all became śramaṇas; with saffron robes upon their bodies, they perfected their dignified deportment.

At that time, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and by the force of their own roots of goodness, the laywomen contemplated with right observation and attained liberation from their female bodies, transforming into men.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, they immediately ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and, with one voice and in unison, spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are entirely like illusions, Arising only from conceptual discrimination;
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), There are no marks of male or female."
A magician, by means of illusory arts,
creates the forms of men and women at a crossroads;
they engage in battle with their armies and all inflict harm upon one another, yet these matters are not real.
I now contemplate birth and death as being no different from an illusion;
they are like the various things a person creates within a dream,
which, having no reality, are seen as nothing at all upon waking.
Contemplate carefully the view of a self: it is nothing but the aggregates, bases, and elements;
it has no real essence and arises solely from inversion.
Just as the moon in the water can be seen but cannot be grasped, so too is the nature of phenomena like the moon in water; in reality, it has no coming or going.
It is also like a mirage in the heat, which appears to have the characteristic of movement.
Or one may see these rivers and ponds, yet they possess no reality.
All phenomena are like mirages; their nature is non-existent.
They arise solely from inversion and ultimately lack a self.
Originally I had a female body, born from inversion;
now observing the male body, it is entirely empty and non-existent.
If one can know emptiness, one should not give rise to discrimination.
Thus, within the emptiness of views, one realizes the body with unimpeded realization.
This is the power of the Buddha’s realm, arising further from past merit;
by also cultivating the dharma present before one, one attains liberation from the female body.
"If there are women who wish to attain a male body,
they should resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), and their aspiration shall be fulfilled. At that time,
the Bodhisattva Who Transformed Her Female Body and Left Home descended from the air, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke to her former husband and the other laymen:
“Good friends!
You all should resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!
It is difficult for a Buddha to appear in the world, and it is likewise extremely difficult not to be born into the various states of suffering;”
To give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of all sentient beings out of great compassion—this too is difficult!
If a person can give rise to the bodhicitta, they thereby make offerings to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Then the bhikṣus said to the bodhisattvas who had transformed their female bodies:
"All of you are our great spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); you are able to teach and transform us, having resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of all sentient beings."
We now, before the Buddha, resolve to attain bodhicitta; we vow that in future ages we shall become Buddhas, exactly like the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had transformed their female bodies addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you grant us the going forth; do not let our ordination follow the method of the ‘Come, O Bhikṣu’ [ordination], nor do we wish to receive the going forth from among the śrāvakas!”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"You should cause these sons of good family to leave the household life in accordance with the Dharma.
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
I shall go forth from the household life.
At that time, the girl Vimalaprabhā went to her mother’s place and said to her:
"Mother, you should resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!
If you, Mother, give rise to this resolve, I shall have repaid your kindness."
The mother said, “I have already resolved my mind! Why is that? Because—”

For ten months you have been within my womb; from that time until now, you have not given rise to thoughts of stinginess, violation of precepts, anger, laziness, distracted mindfulness, evil wisdom, wrong views, greed, hatred, or delusion. You have always been joyful and exultant, with body and mind at peace and happiness, and constantly see in your dreams all the Tathāgatas surrounded by the community of bhikṣus, who preach the Dharma for you.
At that time, I thought to myself:
"The child currently conceived within my womb must surely be a Bodhisattva!
In a dream, I beheld the Tathāgata; with body and mind filled with joy, I immediately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Now that you have exhorted me, I shall follow your words and resolve my mind once again!
At that time, from the girl Vimalaprabhā’s left hand, a most exquisite precious parasol spontaneously emerged. She carried it to her mother and said to her:
"I offer this precious parasol to the Tathāgata; may I make a great vow to serve as a parasol of the Dharma-treasure for all devas and worldlings!"
At that time, Lady Pure Sun took the precious parasol and offered it to the Tathāgata, making this aspiration:
"By these roots of goodness, may I in the future become a parasol of the Dharma-treasure for all devas and worldlings!"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"This girl Vimalaprabhā, sporting with supernatural powers, has come from the buddha-field of the Buddha King Vimalakīrti and manifested in a female body to be born here."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

This woman was originally a bodhisattva named Vimalaprabhā (Stainless Light), who has already attained non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, she has manifested in a female body; it is not due to the influence of past karma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Do you see these seventy-five householder wives who have all become men?
Śāriputra said:
“I have seen them,” [the girl replied]. The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“They were all this girl’s parents in a previous life.”
"Śāriputra! For a long night, the girl Vimalaprabhā made this vow:
'If there are sentient beings who have been my parents, I shall certainly cause them to never regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

While the number of all the stars in this trichiliocosm is easy to know, the number of those who were the parents of this Woman of Stainless Light in her previous lives—those who, having been exhorted by her, practiced wholesome dharmas and did not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—is difficult to know!"
At that time, the girl Vimalaprabhā came forward, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"If it is true that 'all dharmas are neither male nor female,' may my female body be transformed into that of a man!"

When these words were spoken, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; the female form of the maiden Vimalaprabhā vanished, and she manifested the body of a man, adorned with the marks and signs of perfection.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha:
"O Noble One!
That you are able to perform such Buddha-works even before attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is truly most rare!"
The Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
“It is exactly as you have said!
That the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are adorned with great vows, desiring to benefit and bring all sentient beings to fulfillment, is truly most rare!”
For example, just as all the flowers and leaves of the agalloch tree emit only the fragrance of agalloch,

so too do all the roots of goodness produced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas— even those arising from a single thought— constantly emit the fragrance of the merits of the Buddha-dharma for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When this Dharma was being taught, twelve thousand beings in the assembly gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The great earth shook violently, and the gods in the sky rained down various flowers; celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, as they all spoke these words:
"This Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha has preached the truly pure Dharma!"

If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma and, with deep resolve, believe in and rejoice in it, they shall attain great majestic power, be freed from all calamities and hardships, and cultivate various virtuous deeds.
If any woman hears this sutra, you should know that this present body will be her very last.

Why is this? Because this sutra extensively explains the various faults and afflictions of the female body, and also extensively explains the various practices for attaining the pure dharmas that lead to liberation from the female body.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive and uphold this sutra; read, recite, and master it thoroughly, explain it to others, and cause it to be widely disseminated."
Why is this so? Ānanda!

If there were a woman who, having filled Jambudvīpa with various kinds of precious jewels, offered them as a gift to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and sought to escape the female body through those roots of goodness;
Furthermore, if there are women who, upon hearing this sutra, believe, understand, and rejoice, and through those roots of goodness seek to leave behind their female bodies— Ānanda,
you should know that merely hearing the name of this sutra is already swift progress!
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is the name of this sutra?
How should it be upheld?”
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

This sutra is titled ‘Transforming the Female Body,’ it is also titled ‘The Questions of the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhā,’ and it is further titled ‘The Path of Instruction for the Bodhisattva Anatikīrti. You should mindfully receive and uphold it!”

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha and the bodhisattvas who had gathered from other lands, as well as the parents of Vimalaprabha, the Elder Ānanda, and all the devas, gandharvas, asuras, humans, and non-humans present in the assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they prostrated and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Transformation of the Female Body Spoken by the Buddha
